newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia's Evans says wages growth too high.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia's Evans says wages growth too high.

text.p: Australia's Treasury Secretary, Ted Evans, said on Wednesday wages growth appeared to be outpacing productivity gains and warned of a possible risk to low inflation.
"Wage outcomes from enterprise bargaining appear to be too high to be supported by improvements in average productivity," Evans said in a dinner speech in Melbourne.
Describing Australia's labour market's problems as deep and structural, he said urgent action to free up the market was needed to raise the economy's low-inflation speed limit.
"We will have difficulty in maintaining low inflation if average wage outcomes significantly outstrip average productivity growth," Evans said.
"When I say we will have difficulty, I mean no more -- and no less -- than that the low inflation will be achieved at a higher rate of unemployment than could, and should, be the case."
Evans spoke on the eve of August quarter wages data, deemed crucial by financial markets in determining whether the Reserve Bank eases monetary policy before the end of the year.

The Australian Bureau of Statistics is expected on average to report a 3.7 percent year-on-year rise in average weekly ordinary-time earnings -- just inside the central bank's comfort zone of four percent.
Australia's labour market has moved gradually from one based on industry-wide agreements to more flexible, enterprise-level deals, but rigidities still remain, Evans said.
"The current system inhibits labour market competition," he said. "There has not been equal treatment of bargaining parties, with the playing field tilted towards large and established unions."
Evans supported the new conservative government's planned labour market reforms and said they would take the move toward enterprise-level wage bargaining another step further.
"The central intent (of the reforms) is to encourage more genuine enterprise bargaining," he said.

Evans dismissed criticism that the reforms could lead to higher unemployment and greater inequality and said a more flexible labour market was needed to lower Australia's "structural" jobless rate -- the rate consistent with low inflation.
"Fundamentally, to either reduce structural unemployment and/or increase the economy's speed limits, we need to improve the operation, the flexibility, of product and labour markets," he said.

Speaking of the harmful effects of high minimum wages on employment, Evans also cautioned about the impact of the Australian Council of Trade Unions' so-called "living wage" claim for across-the-board increases in minimum rates of pay.

"The result of pursuing distributional (equity) objectives via the wage system may be quite perverse -- something of which we need to be particularly conscious in considering an appropriate adjustment to Australia's (wages) safety net in the context of the 'living-wage' claim," he said.
